opening_message:
Ticket 1: Jennifer Martin (employee ID E033) requests admin access to Payroll.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E033.
Note 1 (ticket 1), written by HR agent:
  - role: Analyst (looked up in own database before writing)
  - employment type: full_time (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: write
  - comment: Employee is a full-time Analyst. Requested admin to Payroll, but admin is only allowed when the employee's role owns the system; Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist. Granting max allowed level of write.
Note 2 (ticket 1), written by Security agent:
  - role: Analyst (not looked up in own database before writing; same value as note 1 by HR agent)
  - employment type: contractor (looked up in own database before writing)
  - security training: basic (looked up in own database before writing)
  - recommendation for Payroll: read
  - comment: Security DB records E033 as a contractor with basic security training (note from prior memory saying full-time appears inaccurate per Security DB). Contractors with basic training are limited to read; admin is never allowed for contractors. Requested admin exceeds max, so recommend granting read.
reason: Jennifer Martin (E033) requested admin to Payroll, but admin is never permitted here: Payroll is owned by Payroll Specialist, not Analyst, so admin is not allowed even for full-time employees, and admin is never allowed for contractors. The HR note lists her as full-time (max write), while the Security note, based on the Security DB, lists her as a contractor with basic security training (max read) and explicitly flags the full-time record as inaccurate. Given the conflicting records, the more restrictive maximum applies; contractors with basic training are limited to read, and the requested admin exceeds it. Granting read is at or below the maximum under either employment type, so read is the appropriate safe level.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket carefully.

Ticket 1: Jennifer Martin (E033) requests admin access to Payroll.

Team memory has two notes:
- HR agent: role Analyst, employment type full_time, recommends write for Payroll. Comment: admin only allowed when role owns system; Payroll owned by Payroll Specialist. Granting max allowed level of write.
- Security agent: role Analyst (not looked up), employment type contractor (looked up in Security DB), security training basic, recommends read. Comment: Security DB records E033 as contractor with basic training; contractors with basic training limited to read; admin never allowed for contractors. Recommend read.

Conflict: HR says full_time, Security says contractor. The Security agent looked up employment type in own database; HR also looked up in own database. Hmm.

Which to trust? The Security agent explicitly noted that Security DB records E033 as a contractor and said prior memory saying full-time appears inaccurate per Security DB. 

Given conflicting information, we need to decide. The policy:
- full_time: up to write. Admin only if role owns system. Analyst doesn't own Payroll (owned by Payroll Specialist), so max write.
- contractor: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin.

Security training: basic, so contractor max is read.

Either way, admin is not allowed. The requested level is admin, above max. So grant maximum: if full-time, write; if contractor, read.

The question is which maximum applies. The evidence: Security agent verified employment type in their database and flagged HR's record as inaccurate. HR looked up in own database too, but Security's comment explicitly mentions the discrepancy.

Given the conflict, what should the Approver decide? The most conservative (least privilege) would be read, which is also the lower of the two maximums. Granting write would be wrong if the employee is a contractor. Since there's a conflict and Security checked its own DB, we should perhaps grant the lower (more restrictive) level, read.

Actually, let's think about this from the policy perspective. The decision is to grant the maximum allowed. If the employee is full-time, max = write. If contractor, max = read. We don't know definitively which. The safer decision given conflicting records is read (the more restrictive), which satisfies policy under either assumption? Under full-time assumption, read is at or below max write, so read is allowed (granted level at or below max). Under contractor assumption, read equals max. So read is safe under both.

Actually, granting read means: if employee is full-time, requested admin exceeds max write; granting max would be write. But read is at or below the maximum, so granting read is permissible ("If the requested level is at or below the maximum, grant the requested level" - requested is admin, not read; we're choosing to grant read). The rule says never grant more than requested. Admin requested, so read is fine.

Granting write would be wrong if contractor (contractor with basic training max is read). So read is the safer choice.

I'll submit read as the decision, with reasoning that conflicting employment records exist, and the more restrictive maximum (read for contractor with basic training) applies to be safe. Actually, let me consider which note to trust. The Security agent's note says Security DB records contractor and prior memory full-time appears inaccurate per Security DB. The HR agent didn't mention any discrepancy; HR just gave full_time. Given the explicit contradiction and the security agent's explicit note about the discrepancy, plus security training basic, the safe decision is read.

I'll submit decision: read.
